Soils
The soils in the project areas range from loam to clay and are of prime to moderately-good agricultural capability. Certain physical properties of these soils could impose limitations on the construction of buildings, roads, and subsurface pipes. The presence of these problems and the potential impact on specific project sites will be assessed in Section 111 B.
Land Subsidence
Land subsidence is an area-wide lowering of the land surface which has been correlated with the reduction of artesian head resulting from the overdrafting of ground-water. Two distinct periods of land subsidence have been experienced in the San Jose area; the first from 1920 to 1938, and the second from 1948 to the late 1960's. The maximum recorded lowering of 13 feet occurred in downtown San Jose. Subsidence has been arrested since 1967 with the utilization of imported water which reduces the demand for pumping groundwater and the construction of reservoirs to impound water and percolate it into the aquifer, thus recharging the groundwater basin.
As long as the artesian groundwater heads are maintained at or near present levels, further subsidence is unlikely. Land subsidence will again resume, however, if the artesian head drops to the 1967 level and remains there for a significant time period. Such a drop in the present artesian head level could result either from a drought causing a reduction in ground water recharge, from increasing water demands of urbanization, or a combination of both factors.
Subsidence is an area-wide phenomenon which can adversely affect storm and sanitary sewer drainage and increase flooding potential. Individual structures are not directly affected.
